background.definition: Partial or complete obstruction of the small bowel (SBO) or large bowel (LBO) that results in the failure of intestinal contents to pass through.

list.listitem: A study of hospital discharges from national database estimated over 300,000 hospitalizations in 1994 for lysis of adhesions, resulting in $1.3 billion in expenditure.

Adhesions from previous abdomen or pelvic surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction (SBO) followed by hernias. Following are other causes of SBO: Crohn's disease. Malignant tumors (primary or secondary). Intussusception is a common cause of SBO in the pediatric age group. Large bowel neoplasm is the most common cause for LBO followed by volvulus and complicated diverticulitis. Some rare causes of bowel obstruction are congenital malformations, obstruction by gallstones, feces, meconium, bezoar, radiation stricture. Postoperative ileus and acute colonic pseudo-obstruction can present with same symptomatology, but without any mechanical obstruction.
Mechanical obstruction of bowel can cause proximal intestinal distension due to accumulation of gastrointestinal secretions and gas above the obstruction.

The distension can become severe over time and lead to compression of intestinal lymphatics. This in turn may lead to loss of fluid and consequently dehydration with hemoconcentration. As peristalsis passes through the obstruction it can cause diarrhea distally.
Complete obstruction and strangulated hernia can compromise perfusion, leading to necrosis and perforation of intestine.
Use of hyaluronic acid agents as an adjunct in pelvic surgery may decrease adhesion formation and prevent the deterioration of pre-existing adhesions.B
Compared to open surgery, laparoscopic surgery is associated with lower subsequent rates of adhesive SBOs.B

A poloaxemer-based anti-adhesive (trade name Guardix SG) was shown in an unblinded randomized trial with 214 patients to reduce the likelihood of bowel obstruction following surgery for gastric adenocarcinoma (7.3% vs 20%, p < 0.05). B

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is accurate in diagnosing adults with SBO, with an 83% sensitivity and a 93% specificity; positive and negative likelihood ratios were 11.9 (95% CI 1.2 - 114.9) and 0.2 (0.1 - 0.3), respectively. B
Bowel obstruction requires traditional application of clinical assessment. Technology does not eliminate the need for careful serial examinations.C
Oral water-soluble contrast studies (e.g., gastrografin) can help predict the non-operative resolution of adhesive SBO, but its predictive role for malignant bowel obstruction is uncertain.B
CT scan, abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is recommended when complete obstruction is suspected. B

Air in the colon and rectum on radiologic examination; absence of any obstruction on CT scan
High use of narcotics before admission or during post operative state.
Prominent abdominal symptoms and sometimes rectal bleeding. High risk for cardiac conditions

list.listitem: Bowel obstruction should be suspected in patients presenting with a history of colicky pain, constipation, vomiting, and previous abdominal surgery.
On PE visible peristalsis, distended abdomen, increased bowel sounds, and reduced abdominal wall movements provide moderate evidence of obstruction.
In case of suspected complete or high-grade partial SBO, CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the prefered test.
X-ray, abdomen supine and upright is the second choice in complete SBO.

If intermittent or low-grade SBO is suspected, any of the following tests are equally acceptable depending on institutional preference: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast and with oral water-soluble contrast or oral dilute barium contrast; CT enterography with IV or water density contrast; CT enteroclysis; or X-ray, small bowel follow through or X-ray small bowel enteroclysis.

Oral water-soluble contrast (e.g., gastrografin) appears helpful as a predictive test in patients with adhesive SBO, but without indication for immediate surgery (i.e., without signs and symptoms of strangulation). In this test, 100 ml of water-soluble contrast is given orally or via NG tube and, if the contrast reaches the caecum on a X-ray within 4 to 24 hr, there is a high probability that it is a partial obstruction and can be managed conservatively. If the contrast does not reach the caecum within 24 hr, the bowel obstruction is most likely complete and may need to be managed surgically. This test appears very accurate for prediction of non-operative resolution of SBO (LR+ 25 and LR− 0.03). However, it should not be used in patients who continue to vomit or who do not have empty stomach as it may cause aspiration pneumonia. It can also interfere with interpretation of subsequent CT scans due to high density.
On the other hand, oral water-soluble contrast studies have uncertain benefits for predicting the non-operative resolution of malignant bowel obstruction, based on a Cochrane review.

Another diagnostic and prognostic tool for SBO is the small bowel follow through (SBFT) which utilizes either oral water-soluble contrast or barium and employs serial imaging performed under fluoroscopy to evaluate the entire small bowel and involves active radiologic monitoring of contrast progression through the bowel. A retrospective study of 799 patients with SBO found that SBFT performed early (<48 hours) decrwithin ases length of stay, readmissions, and time from operation to discharge.
Acute contrast enema for suspected LBO is also very accurate (LR+ 48 and LR− 0.04).

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is accurate in diagnosing adults with SBO, with an 83% sensitivity and a 93% specificity; positive and negative likelihood ratios were 11.9 (95% CI 1.2 - 114.9) and 0.2 (0.1 - 0.3), respectively. When performed by resident physicians, accuracy of POCUS was 75.4%, whereas fellows and attendings had a 94% accuracy. BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 diminishes the accuracy. These findings are based on a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (deemed at low risk of bias) involving 433 patients.

A study peforming a secondary analysis of individual patient-level data from a systematic review on POCUS for SBO diagnosis at five academic emergency departments (n = 403) concluded that the most accurate bowel diameter overall for predicting SBO was 2.75 cm (AUC = 0.76, 95% CI 0.71-0.81). The optimal threshold was 2.75 cm for patients under 65 and 2.95 cm for those 65 years and older. Furthermore, the optimal threshold was 2.75 cm for females and 2.95 cm for males. Validation studies are needed to verify the real-world performance of these POCUS cut-offs.
A clinical prediction rule has been developed and validated to identify patients with possible bowel obstruction.

Presence of distended abdomen and/or increased bowel sounds with either vomiting, previous abdominal surgery, history of constipation, or age over 50 provide good evidence in favor of bowel obstruction.
Suspect bowel obstruction in patients presenting with colicky pain, constipation, vomiting, and a history of previous abdominal surgery.
Elderly patients do not present with the classical symptoms of small bowel obstuction and often may be misdiagnosed in the ED Ref A
Patients need to be resuscitated and stabilized with special attention to co morbidities, metabolic dearrangemnts and sepsis. Ref B
Identify place and grade of obstruction by CT abdomen with IV contrast.
Surgical intervention is the definitive approach in complete obstruction and should be considered early in the clinical course. C
IV hydration is the foundation of supportive care. C
Serial examinations for signs of strangulation and necrosis are recommended during conservative treatment of partial obstruction. C
Octreotide can be considered to improve GI symptoms in patients suffering from inoperable bowel obstruction.B

In patients with partial SBO, treatment with water and 500 mg magnesium oxide, 0.3 gm Lactobacillus acidiphilus and 40 mg simethicone through NG tube followed by clamping it for 1 hr reduced the likelihood of surgery (9% vs 24%; NNT = 7; 95% CI 4-52) and shortened length of stay (1 day vs 4.2 days; p < 0.001).

Gastrografin is effective in the treatment of partial SBO and reduces the need of surgery when conservative treatment is ineffective after 48 hr. A study of 35 patients found that 74% treated with gastrografin resolved without surgery in less than 48 hr.
A small RCT (n = 21) found that neostigmine was effective for active reversal of ACPO, with close cardiovascular monitoring (10 of 11 treated compared with 0 of 10 untreated).

If strangulation is suspected, surgery is indicated as soon as possible. Patients with suspected complete or partial small bowel obstruction can be observed and evaluated further. Conservative management is successful in up to 90% patients without signs of peritonitis; however, it is associated with higher recurrence rates than surgical management.
Patients with signs of complete SBO (diagnosed with absence of water-soluble contrast in caecum on abdominal radiograph after 24 hrs) should undergo surgery.

There are no recommended guidelines for surgery or use of IV corticosteroids for the resolution of malignant bowel obstruction in advanced gynecological or GI cancer. However, a small Danish RCT (n = 120) concluded that perioperative high-dose dexamethasone (1 mg/kg) significantly reduces postoperative CRP level, enhances recovery outcomes (i.e., complications, hemodynamics, pulmonary function, fatigue, postoperative mobilization), and lowers 90-day mortality compared to placebo.
Patients with an obstructing right or transverse colon cancer should undergo right or extended right colectomy. A primary ileocolic anastomosis can be performed in the appropriate clinical setting.
For patients with left-sided colonic obstruction, the procedure selected should be individualized.
Presence of volvulus requires surgery.
There are no RCTs evaluating the comparative efficacy and safety of laparoscopic surgery versus open surgery for patients with SBO.

The initial goal is to check the degree of volume depletion, presence of any metabolic derangement, and the need for surgical intervention. Non-operative management is more successful in patients with partial obstruction as compared to complete SBO.

Conservative management involves IV access with fluids for dehydration and NPO status; in patients with gastric distension, a nasogastric tube; foley catheter to monitor urine output; and frequent assessment of the patient for any signs of developing strangulation.
A systematic review of 4 studies found no advantage of nasointestinal tubes over nasogastric tubes for patients with SBO.
Necrosis and perforation of intestine is a life-threatening complication.
Emergent surgery to remove the dead bowel is indicated.
Bowel obstruction is a common surgical emergency. Surgical consultation is advised.
Patients should be monitored as inpatients/ICU.
Vigilance for need for specialized nutrition.
The risk of recurrence of SBO is very high in patients treated non-operatively.B
The recurrence rate for patients operated once for adhesion-related SBO is 18% after 10 years and 29% at 30 years.B

SBO will recur in about 40% of patients treated non-operatively compared to 27% for the patients treated operatively for mechanical obstruction. Time period to recurrence is much shorter in non-operative group (153 days compared to 411 days).B
Level of care should generally be the same as for non-pregnant with attention to selection of diagnostic studies to minimize radiation exposure, if possible.

Intussusception is the most common cause of bowel obstruction in children aged 6 to 36 months. It is usually diagnosed clinically by presence of episodic pain, currant jelly stools, and bilious emesis.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms the diagnosis. Intussusception can be reduced by either air or barium enema. Surgery is indicated in case of irreducibility and perforation.
